Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Waste All Around Us — Spotting and Sharing
periods.textbook_anchor: How is Waste Created? — Recall different activities you and your elders do during the day and share how these create waste (p. 150)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 150 illustration of children and teacher cleaning a park

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 150 and draws attention to the park-cleaning picture. Students look carefully and share what they notice — who is in the picture, what they seem to be doing, and why the park might need cleaning.

Whole-class discussion: Have you ever seen piles of waste near your home or school? Students share examples in their own words. Teacher records a few waste items named by students on the board in two rough columns — things from home, things from school — without correcting or ranking responses.

Students recall the activities they and their elders do during a typical day — cooking, eating, shopping, studying, playing — and think about what waste each activity creates. They share with a partner first, then the class pools ideas. Teacher builds a growing list on the board: vegetable peels, paper scraps, plastic wrappers, pencil shavings, old bottles, tins, and so on.

Closing discussion: 'What do we do with all this waste?' Students offer whatever they have seen or done — dustbins, open piles, sweeping, burning. Teacher acknowledges all observations without resolution, leaving the question genuinely open for the class to carry forward in thought.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify everyday activities as sources of waste and articulate the connection between human actions and waste generation.
periods.section_context: Park-cleaning picture, waste from cooking and eating activities, waste from school activities — old clothes, tins, bottles, paper, vegetable and fruit peels, plastic wrappers, pencil shavings, old batteries.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did any elder at home do something today that made waste — even a tiny bit?' This opens the conversation to grandparents and caregivers and surfaces the idea that waste-making is universal, not a failure.

periods.activity_title: What Happens When Waste Piles Up?
periods.textbook_anchor: Ways to Manage Waste — Observe your surroundings and report on cleanliness (p. 152)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 152 images of unmanaged waste and its effects

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 152 and students study the images together. Teacher asks: 'What do you see happening in each picture?' Students describe what they observe — animals near waste, smoke, stagnant water — before any explanation is offered.

Structured observation walk around the school boundary or visible outdoor area. Students carry their notebooks and note — using quick sketches or single words — any waste they see, where it is, and what kind it is. Back in class, they settle and review their notes.

Students record their findings in two columns: 'What I saw' and 'Where I saw it'. The class then shares: Is our school clean? Do we find waste inside classrooms, on the grounds, outside the gate? Teacher tallies responses on the board without evaluating — the data belongs to the children.

Brief closing discussion drawing on Textbook p. 152: the text mentions that some communities have transformed their surroundings. Students reflect on what the difference might be between a place that manages waste and one that does not. One or two students share a thought; no resolution is imposed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate environment systematically and record evidence of waste and its effects on living things and health.
periods.section_context: School surroundings observation, animals eating plastic, burning plastic and harmful gases, wastewater and mosquitoes, community cleanliness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: While students share their observations, ask: 'Who do you think is responsible for keeping this clean — you, the school, the municipality, everyone?' This opens the civic-responsibility idea the section builds toward.

periods.textbook_anchor: Reduce — Draw a locality, circle waste spots in red, and find out how waste gets there (p. 153)
materials: Crayons or coloured pencils — red essential

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'Reduce' opening from Textbook p. 153 aloud with the class. Students identify the key idea: the best way to manage waste is to create less of it. A few examples are voiced — cloth bags instead of plastic, sharing old toys — and noted on the board.

Students draw their own locality on a fresh page — their street, their neighbourhood, or the area around school. They add landmarks they know: the market, a park, the school gate, a roadside vendor. Then they circle in red any spots where they have seen garbage or wastewater or smoke. Beside each circle they write one or two words naming the waste they saw there.

Students pair up and explain their maps to each other: 'This red circle is near the market because…' They try to answer how the waste got to each spot — did people drop it? Does it come from a nearby activity? Partners listen and may add a question.
Whole-class reflection: 'If you could remove one red circle from your map, which one would you choose and why?' Two or three students share briefly. Maps are kept for students' own reference.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their local environment visually and identify specific sites and sources of waste accumulation.
periods.section_context: Locality drawing, waste spots near markets and streets, sources of garbage and wastewater, avoiding packaged food and plastic bags, cloth bags, buying only what is needed.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As students draw, move around and ask: 'Where does the person who sells vegetables near your home put the leftover peels?' This keeps the inquiry grounded in real, local observation rather than imagination.

periods.activity_title: How Can I Reduce Waste? — Personal Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Reduce — How can you help in reducing waste? (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 153 at the activity prompt. The class briefly recalls the idea from the locality-mapping work — that waste comes from activities, and less buying and less packaging means less waste. Students are reminded of the key examples: cloth bags, shared books, no extra packaging.

Students work individually to think through their own daily routine — morning to night — and list in their notebooks every action they or their family could take to reduce waste. They aim for at least four actions, using their own words. The list is personal — there are no wrong answers.

Small groups of three or four pool their lists. Together they identify the three actions they think would make the biggest difference and write those on a shared page or board space. Each group briefly names their top three to the class.
Class reflection: 'Is it easy to reduce waste, or does it need effort? What makes it hard?' Two or three students respond. Teacher closes by affirming that small, everyday choices add up.

periods.implied_lo: Students can propose specific, actionable strategies to reduce waste generation in their own daily life.
periods.section_context: Avoiding packaged food, using cloth bags, sharing old toys and books, buying only what is needed, reducing household and school waste.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt quieter students with: 'Think about the last time something was bought at your home — did it come with packaging? What happened to that packaging?' This makes the inquiry concrete and personal rather than abstract.

periods.activity_title: Reuse in Action — The Paper Bag
periods.textbook_anchor: Reuse — Make a paper bag using only newspaper, no scissors or glue (p. 155)
materials: One sheet of newspaper per student
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 155 step-by-step paper bag folding diagrams

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 155 and the class reads the reuse introduction together. Teacher draws out the examples: reusing one-sided paper, refilling a steel or copper bottle, making something from old newspapers or calendars. Students are asked: 'Do you know anyone at home who makes something new from an old thing?' A few responses are heard.

Each student takes one newspaper sheet. Using the step-by-step diagrams on Textbook p. 155, students fold their paper bag with no scissors and no glue — the teacher demonstrates each fold once slowly before students attempt it. Students who finish first help a neighbour. The bag must stand open on the desk to be complete.

Students examine their finished bags. Discussion: 'What could you carry in this bag? Could it replace a plastic bag — even once?' Students share two or three uses. Teacher links back to the reuse idea: the newspaper was already used; the bag gives it a second life.
Brief reflection: 'What other things at home could be given a second life instead of being thrown away?' One or two quick responses close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step making process using discarded materials and explain how reuse reduces the need for new resources.
periods.section_context: Newspaper paper bag (no scissors, no glue), reusing one-sided paper, refilling steel or copper bottles, making toys and decorative things from old newspapers, calendars, bottles, boxes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: While students fold, ask: 'Your grandparents or elders — did they ever make something from old cloth or old material instead of buying new?' This surfaces the traditional quilt-from-saree and cloth-bag practices the section describes, naturally and without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: A Gift from Waste — Make and Give
periods.textbook_anchor: Reuse — Create an item using waste material that you can give as a gift to someone (p. 156)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 156 and reads the gift-making activity prompt. Students decide individually who they would like to make a gift for and what the person might enjoy. Teacher asks: 'What materials do we have here that were already used or would otherwise be thrown away?' Students survey the materials on the desk.

Students design and make their gift item using only the available waste materials. Possible outcomes: a folded newspaper basket, a decorated cardboard box, a rolled-paper pen holder, a small envelope from an old calendar page. The teacher circulates, asking each student to explain their design choice and who it is for.

Gallery walk: students place their items on their desks and move quietly around to see each other's work. Each maker stands by their item for a moment and can say one sentence about it if they choose.

Closing thought: 'When you give this to someone, what will you tell them about how it was made?' One or two students share. Teacher affirms that a handmade gift from waste carries meaning beyond its material.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and create a usable object from discarded materials, demonstrating that reused materials retain value.
periods.section_context: Gift item made from waste materials — newspapers, old calendars, cardboard boxes, old cloth; quilts from old sarees, bags from old cloth as traditional reuse examples.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student is unsure what to make, prompt: 'Think of something the person uses every day — could you make a version of that from what's here?' Keep the focus on the waste material being transformed, not on a perfect finished product.

periods.activity_title: Places of Pride — Inquiry from Elders
periods.textbook_anchor: A Place of Pride — Ask your elders about any village, town or city known for its cleanliness and share with the class (p. 157)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 157 images and text about Silluk village, Chhota Narena, Indore, Mysuru

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 157 and reads the section aloud. Students hear about Silluk village in Arunachal Pradesh, Chhota Narena, Indore, and Mysuru. Teacher pauses after each place: 'Has anyone heard of this place? Does your family come from near there?' Two or three students respond if they have a connection.

Students share what they found out from elders at home — or what they know from their own experience — about a clean place. Each student who shares names the place, says what makes it clean or well-managed, and how they know. Teacher writes place names on the board as they come up.

Class discussion: What do the clean places described have in common? Students suggest patterns — people work together, there are rules, people care. Teacher asks: 'Could our school area become a place of pride? What would it take?' Students discuss in pairs, then share one idea each.

Teacher introduces the Swachh Bharat Mission briefly from Textbook p. 157 — a national programme that supports communities in becoming cleaner. Students note the name in their notebooks. Closing question: 'What is one thing a whole community has to do together that one person alone cannot do?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can gather information through community inquiry and connect local examples of cleanliness to broader patterns of collective civic effort.
periods.section_context: Silluk village (zero waste village, Arunachal Pradesh), Chhota Narena, Indore, Mysuru, Swachh Bharat Mission, elders' knowledge of clean places.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If no student has information from home, ask: 'Has anyone visited a place that felt very clean and well-looked-after? What made it feel that way?' This keeps the inquiry alive even when the homework task was not completed, per the self-contained unit requirement.

periods.activity_title: Green Bin or Blue Bin? — Sorting Waste
periods.textbook_anchor: Separate Different Types of Waste — Write the names of waste materials that go into each dustbin (p. 159)
materials: Green and blue crayons or coloured pencils

A collection of clean waste items from the classroom: paper scraps, a plastic bottle cap, a dried leaf, an orange peel (or any fruit peel), an egg shell, a small piece of glass or metal if safe, a piece of cardboard
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 159 illustration of green and blue dustbins

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 159. Students look at the two dustbin drawings. Teacher asks: 'What colour are the two bins? Has anyone seen coloured dustbins — in school, on the street, at a park?' Students share observations. Teacher introduces the rule: green for things that rot, blue for things that can be remade.

Teacher places the collected waste items on a central table one at a time. For each item, students decide — by raising a green or blue card (or coloured paper slip) — which bin it belongs to. After each decision the class checks against Textbook p. 159 and a student explains the reasoning: 'The dried leaf goes in green because it will rot and become compost.'

Students open their notebooks and draw two dustbins — one green, one blue. Using Textbook p. 159 as reference, they write the names of waste materials inside each bin. They add at least two items from their own home or school that are not pictured in the textbook.

Quick class check: teacher calls out a waste item; students call out the bin colour. Items include a glass bottle, a banana peel, a newspaper, an egg shell, a plastic bag. Errors are corrected by the class, not just the teacher.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify waste materials as organic or recyclable and explain the system for correctly sorting them into colour-coded bins.
periods.section_context: Green bin (organic waste — dried leaves, fruit peels, vegetable waste, egg shells, compost), blue bin (recyclable materials — metal, glass, plastic, paper), colour-coded dustbin system.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone's home or neighbourhood already use coloured bins? What do people actually put in them — is it always correct?' This surfaces real local practice and opens space to notice gaps without blame.

periods.activity_title: Cleaning Tools and Actions — List, Draw, Reflect
periods.textbook_anchor: Keeping our Surroundings Clean — List tools used for cleaning in school or neighbourhood and draw them (p. 160)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 160 illustration and writing prompts

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 160. Students read the two writing prompts together: things that keep home and classroom clean, and tools used for cleaning. Teacher asks: 'Close your eyes for a moment — picture someone cleaning your home or your street. What are they using?' Students name tools aloud: broom, mop, dustpan, bucket, scrubber, garbage cart.

Students write their two lists in their notebooks: first, actions they can take to keep their home and classroom clean; second, tools they have seen used in school or the neighbourhood. They aim for at least four items in each list. Teacher circulates and asks individual students to say one item they are proud to have thought of.

Students draw at least three cleaning tools in the box on Textbook p. 160 or in their notebooks — drawn clearly enough that a reader would know what the tool is and what it does. They label each drawing with the tool's name.

Brief share: each student shows one drawing to a neighbour and names the tool and who in their home or neighbourhood uses it. Closing thought: 'Are some of these tools used by people whose work we don't always notice? How can we show that we value their work?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and represent cleaning tools and practices used in their home and community, recognising those who perform cleaning work.
periods.section_context: Cleaning tools in home and school — broom, mop, dustpan, bucket, garbage cart; actions to keep home and classroom clean; people who clean in school and neighbourhood.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students share who uses the tools, gently ask: 'Is cleaning work done by everyone at home, or mostly by some people? Is that fair?' This opens a values conversation about dignity of labour without prescribing an answer.

periods.activity_title: Want Not, Waste Not — Pledge, Poster, and Role Play
periods.textbook_anchor: Keeping our Surroundings Clean — Make a poster of a village or town managing waste well, and role-play a clean town and a dirty town conversation (p. 161)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 161 poster prompt and p. 162 role-play prompt

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the motto 'Want not, Waste not' from Textbook p. 161 aloud. Students repeat it and discuss in pairs: what does it mean to 'want not'? What does it mean to 'waste not'? Two or three pairs share. Teacher links it to the whole chapter's journey — from noticing waste, to reducing and reusing it, to separating it and keeping surroundings clean.

Students make a poster on Textbook p. 161 or a drawing sheet showing a village or town that is managing its waste well. The poster must have a title they choose themselves. It can show green and blue bins, clean streets, people separating waste, trees, clean water — whatever they imagine a well-managed place looks like.

Role play in pairs from Textbook p. 162: one partner is a clean town, the other a dirty town. They hold a short conversation — the clean town describes how it feels and what it does; the dirty town describes its problems and asks for advice. After a few minutes, partners may swap roles if they wish.

Whole-class closing: each student silently writes one personal action they commit to — one thing they will do differently. Teacher reads the National Cleanliness Day pledge idea from Textbook p. 161 and invites students to read their personal commitment aloud if they wish. No student is compelled to share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate a personal commitment to waste reduction and express an understanding of a clean community through creative and dramatic forms.
periods.section_context: Poster of a clean village or town, role play of clean town and dirty town, personal pledge, National Cleanliness Day (30 January), motto 'Want not Waste not', zero-waste birthday party discussion, waste in nature.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: During the role play, listen for students who naturally bring in specific ideas from the chapter — green bins, cloth bags, reusing newspaper — and acknowledge these: 'You just brought in something we explored carefully. Well done.' This reinforces transfer.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya's family cooks food every day. Which of the following is waste that is most likely created by cooking?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This item checks whether the student can link a specific everyday activity (cooking) to the waste it produces — the core idea of the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify everyday activities as sources of waste and articulate the connection between human actions and waste generation.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates waste with a different everyday activity (using electronics) rather than identifying cooking as the source — shows a narrow or confused understanding of waste origins.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student connects waste to school activities (writing) rather than the home cooking activity in the question — shows partial understanding limited to one context.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recalls waste from the section's list (old clothes) but does not connect it to the specific activity named — shows recall without application.

assessment_items.question_text: Unmanaged waste can cause harm to animals and people. Name two ways in which unmanaged waste harms living things, and for each harm, name the type of waste that causes it.
expected_elements: One harm to animals — for example, animals (such as cows) eating plastic waste and getting injured or dying.
One harm to people — for example, wastewater or stagnant water near waste breeding mosquitoes and spreading disease, or burning plastic releasing harmful gases people breathe.
For each harm, the type of waste named (plastic / wastewater / burning waste).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each correctly named harm linked to its waste type. Partial credit: one complete harm-and-waste pair is sufficient for half marks. Regional examples of local waste problems are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate environment systematically and record evidence of waste and its effects on living things and health.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

expected_elements: One harm to animals — for example, animals (such as cows) eating plastic waste and getting injured or dying.
One harm to people — for example, wastewater or stagnant water near waste breeding mosquitoes and spreading disease, or burning plastic releasing harmful gases people breathe.
For each harm, the type of waste named (plastic / wastewater / burning waste).

assessment_items.task: Think about the area around your home or school. Draw a simple map or picture of that place. Use a red circle to mark any spot where you have seen garbage, dirty water, or smoke. Below your drawing, write one sentence for each red circle explaining how waste got to that spot.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My map shows: [draw here]
Red circle 1 is near __________ because __________.
Red circle 2 is near __________ because __________.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn map or locality picture with at least one red circle
At least one written sentence explaining how waste reached the circled spot
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response shows a recognisable locality with at least one red circle placed at a real or plausible spot, and a sentence that names a human activity as the cause. Regional variation in the places drawn and the waste described is expected and should be accepted.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their local environment visually and identify specific sites and sources of waste accumulation.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate direct environmental observation into a visual representation and link waste locations to human activity — combining spatial thinking with causal reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides without restricting: the student fills in a location and a cause. Accept any real or plausible location the student knows. The sentence need not be grammatically perfect — the causal link ('because') is what matters.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: map shows a specific, recognisable place; red circles are at plausible waste sites; sentence names a concrete activity (e.g. 'because people drop packaging from the market'). Weak: map is generic or unlabelled; red circle has no explanation; sentence merely restates 'there is garbage there'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their map in words or dictate it. Students in rural and urban settings will draw very different localities — both are correct. A student with one red circle and one strong sentence meets the task fully.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the mode the textbook uses for this task; it allows students without strong writing fluency to demonstrate spatial and observational thinking.

assessment_items.question_text: Write two specific actions you can take in your daily life to reduce waste. For each action, explain what kind of waste it will reduce.
expected_elements: Two distinct, specific actions (not vague statements like 'don't waste').
For each action, a named type of waste it reduces — e.g. using a cloth bag reduces plastic bag waste; sharing old books reduces paper or book waste.
Actions should be things the student can genuinely do, not things only an adult can do.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per complete action-and-waste pair, up to two marks. Accept any reasonable, culturally appropriate action the student names — region-specific alternatives (e.g. using a jute bag, a steel tiffin) are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can propose specific, actionable strategies to reduce waste generation in their own daily life.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Two distinct, specific actions (not vague statements like 'don't waste').
For each action, a named type of waste it reduces — e.g. using a cloth bag reduces plastic bag waste; sharing old books reduces paper or book waste.
Actions should be things the student can genuinely do, not things only an adult can do.

assessment_items.question_text: You folded a paper bag from a single sheet of newspaper using no scissors and no glue. Explain in two or three sentences how making this bag is an example of reuse and how it helps reduce waste.
expected_elements: Identification that the newspaper was already used (printed) and is being given a new use rather than thrown away.
A statement that this means fewer plastic or paper bags need to be bought or made — linking reuse to resource saving.
An explanation that using the bag means less waste is generated from packaging.
assessment_items.annotation: Full marks for a response that connects 'used material given new purpose' to 'less waste created'. Partial credit for identifying that newspaper is being reused without explaining the waste-reduction benefit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step making process using discarded materials and explain how reuse reduces the need for new resources.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Identification that the newspaper was already used (printed) and is being given a new use rather than thrown away.
A statement that this means fewer plastic or paper bags need to be bought or made — linking reuse to resource saving.
An explanation that using the bag means less waste is generated from packaging.

assessment_items.task: Using only waste materials you can find in your classroom right now (paper scraps, old newspaper, cardboard), make a small useful object — something someone could use or keep. When you are done, write one sentence on the object (or on a label attached to it) saying what it is made from and who you would give it to.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My object is a __________.
It is made from: __________.
I would give it to __________ because __________.
format_of_output: A small handmade object from waste materials
A written label or sentence on or attached to the object
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student has used genuinely discarded material, produced something with a clear intended use, and articulated the material source. The object need not be elaborate — a folded envelope, a pen holder, a small box all qualify. Region-specific materials are welcome.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and create a usable object from discarded materials, demonstrating that reused materials retain value.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can transform discarded material into a purposeful object and articulate the reuse principle in a concrete, personal way.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks for three things: what the object is, what it is made from, and who it is for. A student who completes all three demonstrates both making and reflecting. Accept any intended recipient.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: object has a clear form and purpose; label names the waste material specifically (e.g. 'made from a cereal box') and a real intended recipient. Weak: object is an unformed scrap with no identifiable purpose; label is absent or says only 'waste'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students with limited dexterity may produce a simpler object — a flat, folded piece with a label still demonstrates the concept. Students may describe their intended object in words if making is not possible in the time available.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task asks students to create a gift item from waste material — the three-dimensional product with an annotation directly parallels the task and demonstrates making as a mode of expression.

assessment_items.question_text: Silluk village in Arunachal Pradesh is called a 'zero waste village'. Which of the following best explains why a whole community, not just one person, is needed to achieve this?

options.label: A
options.text: Because only the village head has the authority to set rules about waste.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the government sends people to clean the village every day.

options.label: C
options.text: Because waste is created by everyone's activities, managing it well requires everyone to act together.

options.label: D
options.text: Because zero waste means no one in the village ever creates any waste at all.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests whether the student understands that civic cleanliness requires collective action — the core idea the section develops through the example of model villages.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather information through community inquiry and connect local examples of cleanliness to broader patterns of collective civic effort.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student interprets community effort as authority-based rather than participatory — misses the idea that every member contributes, not just a leader.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student attributes cleanliness to external government intervention rather than the community's own shared action — contradicts the section's model of local responsibility.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student takes 'zero waste' literally to mean no waste is ever produced, rather than understanding it as effective community waste management — a factual misconception.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these waste items: a banana peel, an old newspaper, a glass bottle, a dry leaf, a plastic bottle cap, a metal tin. Sort each item into the correct bin by writing its name under 'Green Bin' or 'Blue Bin'. Then, for the green bin items, write one sentence explaining what happens to them after they are collected.
expected_elements: Green Bin: banana peel, dry leaf (organic items that rot and become compost).
Blue Bin: old newspaper, glass bottle, plastic bottle cap, metal tin (recyclable materials).
One sentence for green bin items: they rot / decompose and become compost / nutrients for soil.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for correct sorting of all six items (accept five of six for partial credit). Award one mark for the compost / decomposition sentence. Full marks: 2. The item directly tests the classification system taught through the colour-coded bin activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify waste materials as organic or recyclable and explain the system for correctly sorting them into colour-coded bins.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Green Bin: banana peel, dry leaf (organic items that rot and become compost).
Blue Bin: old newspaper, glass bottle, plastic bottle cap, metal tin (recyclable materials).
One sentence for green bin items: they rot / decompose and become compost / nutrients for soil.

assessment_items.task: In your notebook, draw at least three tools that people use to keep their home or school clean. Label each drawing with the tool's name. Below your drawings, write one sentence about a person in your home, school, or neighbourhood who uses one of these tools and whose cleaning work helps everyone.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Tool 1: [draw and label]
Tool 2: [draw and label]
Tool 3: [draw and label]
The person I am writing about is __________. They use __________ to clean __________. Their work helps because __________.
format_of_output: At least three labelled drawings of cleaning tools
One written sentence about a person who uses one of the tools
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether drawings are recognisable and labelled, and whether the sentence identifies a real person and explains the benefit of their work. Region-specific tools (e.g. a jhadu, a phawda, a kartoos) are correct and should be welcomed. The person named may be anyone — a family member, a school cleaner, a municipality worker.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and represent cleaning tools and practices used in their home and community, recognising those who perform cleaning work.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can represent observed tools visually and in writing, and connect cleaning work to the people who perform it — developing recognition of community contributors.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the student through tool, user, and benefit. Accept local names for tools. The sentence need not be grammatically complete — the identification of a person and their contribution is the substance.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three distinct, recognisable tools drawn and named (including local names); sentence names a specific real person and explains why their work matters ('the didi who sweeps keeps us from getting sick'). Weak: three identical or unrecognisable drawings with no labels; sentence names a tool but no person or benefit.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe the tool in words in the label box. Students in different regions will name different tools — a jhadu, a bucket, a long-handled scrubber, a garbage cart are all valid. No tool is more correct than another.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task uses drawing as the mode for representing cleaning tools, making it the natural assessment format for this period's implied learning outcome.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine you are planning a birthday party at your home. Think about all the waste a birthday party usually creates. Write a short paragraph (four to six sentences) explaining how you would make it a 'zero-waste' birthday party — what choices you would make and why each choice helps reduce waste.
look_for: Identification of at least two specific types of waste a birthday party creates (e.g. plastic plates/cups, decorations, food packaging, wrapping paper, plastic balloons).
At least two specific waste-reduction choices linked to those waste types (e.g. using cloth napkins, real plates, newspaper-wrapped gifts, home-cooked food to avoid packaging, reusable decorations).
A clear explanation of why each choice reduces waste — not just listing choices but reasoning about them.
A personal commitment or perspective: the student positions themselves as the decision-maker, not an observer.
Use of chapter vocabulary or ideas: reduce, reuse, less packaging, cloth instead of plastic, or similar.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an evaluative reasoning item. Strong responses show that the student has internalised the reduce-reuse logic and can apply it to a new, personal scenario. Award marks in bands: full marks for responses meeting four or more look-for markers; partial for two or three; minimal for one. Accept any party context — the scenario is universal but the specific choices may vary by region (e.g. leaf plates, jute bags for return gifts).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate a personal commitment to waste reduction and express an understanding of a clean community through creative and dramatic forms.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Identification of at least two specific types of waste a birthday party creates (e.g. plastic plates/cups, decorations, food packaging, wrapping paper, plastic balloons).
At least two specific waste-reduction choices linked to those waste types (e.g. using cloth napkins, real plates, newspaper-wrapped gifts, home-cooked food to avoid packaging, reusable decorations).
A clear explanation of why each choice reduces waste — not just listing choices but reasoning about them.
A personal commitment or perspective: the student positions themselves as the decision-maker, not an observer.
Use of chapter vocabulary or ideas: reduce, reuse, less packaging, cloth instead of plastic, or similar.
